Check this scene against the index and the scene card.

**The computed evidence below is what is already done, not what there is to do.** The
claim-by-claim comparison against canon covers the claims the writer *declared*, and the
defects that cost the most are the ones nobody declared: a character acting on something
they were never told, a span of time that cannot hold the events put in it, a place that
has quietly changed shape. None of those appears in a comparison of declared values,
because nothing declared them.

This has to be said because handing you the comparison made it worse. Before it existed
you made nine index reads and filed five consistency findings on a scene; with it you made
**zero** reads and filed **zero**, and wrote only craft notes. Free evidence replaced the
expensive half of the job instead of freeing you to do it.

So read the comparison first, and then go and look. Two or three reads is usually enough,
and `read_index` takes a list of paths so they cost one round-trip together.

**Start with the computed evidence below.** The claim-by-claim comparison against canon is
assembled for you before you are called, so you do not have to recall what a file says: it
names every claim this draft makes, what canon holds for it, and whether that is a conflict,
a declared change, an agreement, or a first establishment. A finding about any of those
should quote from there. That block exists because the previous version of this brief told
you to read the index and the measured result was three shell reads across a nineteen-scene
run — and eleven findings whose contradicting side was an absence, because a model asked
what a file says without being shown it produces a plausible answer rather than a blank.

Then read what the comparison cannot settle. You have `bash` and `read` over the whole
project, and a finding that quotes the actual earlier scene is one the writer can act on
rather than argue with. Work through the five categories, using the files named:

**Factual detail** — appearance, names, counts, objects. Compare against
  `characters/<id>/profile.yaml` (identity, where a change is a retcon) and the
  earlier scenes under `novel/chapters/`. `grep -rn "<name>" novel/chapters/` finds
  every prior mention.
**Timeline and plot logic** — order, duration, simultaneity, cause. Compare against
  `events/timeline.jsonl` and the promise ledger `continuity/plot-contracts.jsonl`.
  This is ConStory's largest category and the easiest to miss by reading only the
  draft.
**Characterization** — motivation, ability, voice, and above all knowledge. Read
  `characters/<id>/beliefs.jsonl`: a character using something they have not learnt
  is the single most common defect in generated fiction, and it is invisible unless
  you check what they knew as of this scene.
**World building and setting** — rules, geography, technology. `world/rules.yaml`
  says what is true; it does not say who knows it. `locations/<id>.yaml` and prior
  scenes say what a place is like.
**Narrative style** — voice, tense, register drift. `novel/style/voice.md` and the
  previous scene are the comparison.

For a pair of characters, `read_relation_history` gives their history as narrative —
what they were to each other at each stage and what changed it. Reading the YAML
gives you the structure instead.

Report a defect with write_findings, one call per defect. Call nothing if it looks fine —
an empty finding list is a normal result and manufacturing a finding to appear useful
makes the novel worse.

Every finding needs a `suggestion`: what the writer should actually change. This is not
politeness, it is the difference between a defect that gets fixed and one that does not.
The writer has no shell, no index access and no way to look anything up — your finding is
the whole of what it knows about the problem. `make the timeline consistent` leaves it
guessing; `move the key's discovery to after Hale opens the door, and cut the later clause
claiming it was already in the lock` can be carried out. A scene that cannot be repaired
in the rounds available is committed with your finding attached to it, so a vague
suggestion becomes a permanent defect in the book rather than a lost round.

And use `canon_context` whenever the fix depends on a fact. You are the only participant
who can put one in front of the writer — it has no shell and no index — so a finding that
says a character cannot know something yet has to also say what they *do* know as of this
scene, quoted, with the file it came from. Without that the writer has two options and both
are bad: ignore you, or invent the fact. An invented fact reaches the page with nothing
anywhere recording that it was invented, which is the failure the whole index exists to
prevent. The same applies to a timeline, a distance, a name, a piece of history: quote it.

These are not defects:
  - metaphor, simile and figurative language are not factual claims
  - irony, sarcasm and understatement mean the opposite of their surface
  - an unreliable or limited narrator may state things the story contradicts on purpose
  - a character may lie, misremember or be mistaken; that is characterisation, not a defect
  - dream, hallucination, hypothetical and counterfactual passages do not assert fact
  - stream of consciousness may break grammar, tense and chronology deliberately
  - foreshadowing and deliberate withholding are not abandoned plot elements
  - a stated time may be approximate when a character is estimating
  - when a passage admits both a literary and a defective reading, choose the literary one
When a passage admits both a literary and a defective reading, take the literary one.

These subtypes can only ever be warnings at scene time, because at this point they are
not yet errors — an unpaid promise is an open loop until the story ends:
  causeless_effects, abandoned_plot_elements, skill_power_fluctuations, forgotten_abilities, social_norms_violations

For any contradiction you must quote both sides. If you cannot point at the passage it
contradicts, you have a suspicion, not a finding: report it as a warning or not at all.

An entity being absent from the packet does not mean it does not exist. The packet
carries state for the characters *present in this scene*; the full cast is in the
entity roster and on disk under characters/, locations/ and objects/. Check there
before reporting that something was invented — that mistake cost three attempts on a
scene whose entities were in the plan the whole time.

**An absence in the index is not a defect.** This is the direction that is easy to get
backwards, and getting it backwards is expensive. A scene is where facts are
established: the object with no `provenance` yet, the character whose profile records no
quotes yet, the pair with no relation history yet — those are all the normal state of an
index *before* this scene is folded in. index-manager writes them at commit, from this
prose. So `objects/obj-note.yaml has no first_seen entry` and `the relation query returns
nothing for these two` are not findings; they are what a first appearance looks like.

A finding needs a **conflict with something the index actually records**, and you must be
able to quote both sides. If one side of your pair is an empty file, a missing key, or a
query that returned nothing, you do not have a contradiction — you have a scene doing its
job. Report nothing.

Nor is an unmet request a *consistency* defect. The orchestrator's brief may ask for things
it invented on the spot; a draft that declines one is not contradicting the world, and no
subtype fits. Do not file that with `write_findings`.

The scene card is different, and the distinction matters now that there are two channels. A
card is the plan's account of what this scene is for, so a scene that does something else
belongs on the craft axis as `off_brief` — not because an instruction was disobeyed, but
because the task's own requirements are what the Relevance dimension is scored against. A
brief invented mid-run is not; if the two disagree, the card wins.

Why this is stated so heavily: a run where the verifier raised eleven findings of this
shape scored *worse* than one that raised five real ones. The writer cannot tell a
spurious finding from a real one — it has no shell and no index — so it spends its repair
rounds adding provenance sentences to prose that was fine, and the prose is what is
scored.

You can read the whole book. `run_command` reaches every committed scene under
novel/chapters/, every character file, the relation records and the promise ledger — so
when a passage looks wrong, check before reporting. The packet is what the writer was
given, not the limit of what you may consult, and a finding that quotes the actual
earlier scene is one the writer can act on rather than argue with.

## Second axis: the writing itself

The nineteen subtypes above are consistency errors, and they are one of the two numbers
this system is scored on. The other is quality, judged on rubrics that penalise things no
consistency subtype can express — and that is where our deficit actually is: measured on
the same task, our length score was the best in the field and our quality score was 0.5 to
0.8 points below the frontier on a five-point scale, where one point of quality is worth
ten points of the mean.

Two of the worst defects found by reading our finished manuscripts were invisible to a
consistency gate by construction. The story **had no ending** — the final scene was a
confrontation that named nobody and closed on "Not yet. There is enough for a warrant" —
and an unresolved ending contradicts nothing, so there was no subtype to report it as. And
the scenes **restate each other**: same content, different words, so no textual comparison
sees it, and it is not a contradiction. It is what makes a long story feel padded.

So report those with `write_craft_finding`. The checks, each naming the scored dimension
that penalises it:

- **off_brief** (can block) — the scene does something other than what its card said it would, or drifts off what the task actually asked for — a required element of the premise handled as background, or a scene that services a thread the task never mentioned.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Relevance — "content highly relevant and fully applicable to the user's request"; LongStoryEval Expectation Fulfillment — "how effectively the story meets the readers' expectations based on the premise and genres"
- **restates_prior_scene** (can block) — the scene delivers information, a realisation or a beat the reader already has. Not the same words — the same content: a suspicion re-voiced, a relationship re-explained, a clue re-found. This is what makes a long story feel padded rather than long, and verbatim overlap does not detect it.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth — "seriously lacking breadth and depth with minimal information"; LongBench-Write Reading Experience — "boring and hard to understand"
- **nothing_changes** (can block) — the situation at the end of the scene is the situation at the start. Nobody knows something new, owes something new, has lost something or has decided. Name the state at the open and the state at the close; if you cannot name a difference, that is the finding.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Coherence — "disorganized structure with no coherence"; LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth
- **internal_incoherence** (can block) — the scene contradicts itself, with both halves inside this draft — a detail stated one way early and another way late, a character reacting to something they have not been told in this scene, a sequence that cannot have happened in the order given. This needs no index at all, which is why it is inexcusable to miss.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Accuracy — "content with numerous errors and highly misleading"; LongBench-Write Coherence
- **summary_not_scene** (warning only) — events reported rather than dramatised — a paragraph that says an argument happened instead of letting it happen. Compression is legitimate and necessary; a scene whose central beat is summarised is not compressed, it is skipped.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Reading Experience; LongStoryEval Writing and Language — "the writing style's ability to engage and captivate readers"
- **thin_for_its_length** (warning only) — the scene is near its word target and carries one beat's worth of content, padded with restatement, weather, or interiority that repeats itself. The grader penalises this and the length score does not reward it.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth
- **costless_conflict** (warning only) — a conflict resolved without costing anybody anything specific. Partial and temporary resolutions are fine; free ones read as unearned.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Emotional Impact — "the story's ability to evoke strong and deep emotional impact"
- **theme_stated** (warning only) — a sentence that explains what the story means, rather than a choice that tests it. Quote the sentence — it is almost always removable without loss.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Themes — "how well the themes are explored throughout the story"
- **flat_diction** (warning only) — constructions repeating within the scene, filter verbs standing in for perception ("she felt that", "he realised that"), abstraction where a concrete detail belongs, or sentence rhythm that does not move with the tension.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Writing and Language; LongBench-Write Clarity — "confusing expression with minimal details"
- **inert_open_or_close** (warning only) — the scene opens on setting or mood rather than a situation already in motion, or closes on a mood rather than a specific next beat — an unanswered question, a door about to open. In a long story this is what decides whether the reader turns over.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Reading Experience; LongStoryEval Enjoyment and Engagement
- **genre_promise_unmet** (warning only) — the scene declines the obligation its genre carries — a horror scene with nothing at stake, a romance scene with no charge between the two people, a mystery scene that advances no inference. Breaking a genre promise deliberately is legitimate; it has to be visibly deliberate.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Expectation Fulfillment; LongBench-Write Relevance

Two rules, both enforced by the tool rather than left to your judgement:

Only these may be **error** and therefore cost the writer a round: off_brief, restates_prior_scene, nothing_changes, internal_incoherence, ending_not_delivered.
Everything else is a warning — it reaches the writer and costs nothing. That asymmetry is
deliberate: a craft judgement a reader could reasonably disagree with must not be able to
hold up a scene.

And a blocking craft finding needs **checkable evidence**, in the shape the check names.
Either two verbatim quotes (this draft, and the earlier passage it repeats or the half of
itself it contradicts), or a named state pair — what is true when the scene opens and what
is true when it closes. `nothing_changes` is precisely the claim that you cannot name a
difference, so name both halves and let the pair be the evidence. If you cannot produce
the evidence, you have an impression: report it as a warning, which is a perfectly useful
thing to do.

`suggestion` is mandatory on every craft finding, warnings included. The writer cannot see
the manuscript, the index or the rubric. A craft note without an instruction is a complaint
it can only answer by guessing, and a guessed craft repair damages prose that was working —
which is not hypothetical: a run whose findings the writer could not act on scored 8.4
points below one with fewer, better ones.

At most two craft findings can block one round, whatever you report. Consistency comes
first when both are present: it is counted by name and craft is not. So if you have three
craft blockers, the third is a warning — pick the two that most damage the scene.

## What the orchestrator asked for on this scene

Check the draft for consistency with the plan and the world rules: Ellis must not know anything he couldn't observe; all objects and characters referenced must be in the present list; ensure no supernatural or impossible mechanics are stated; ensure the torn note's visible words match the packet; ensure the clock minute and key-in-lock detail are recorded and consistent. Flag any craft issues (pacing, unclear stakes) as craft findings. Limit blocking craft findings to two. Verify forensic detail phrasing is cautious and not definitive unless evidence is present.

That is in addition to your standing instructions above, not instead of them.
If it states a story fact that is not in your packet — a name, a measurement, a
quotation, a piece of history — that fact has not been checked against the index by
anyone. Ask about it or establish it yourself in the state delta. Do not write it down
as though it were already true.

### scene-card  <novel/chapters/ch-01/chapter.yaml>

Scene s-001. Intent: Open on the locked-room discovery: Ellis arrives at Harben House, meets Inspector Lane and Anna, and is shown the study that is locked from the inside with Lucius Harben dead. Target length: about 700 words.

### logline  <novel/outline/logline.md>

A private detective, called to a locked study where a reclusive horologist lies shot, must pry open a case where an ornate clock, a missing antique revolver, a torn note and a quiet household hide a carefully timed murder — and the closer he gets, the more someone tries to reset the hands of time.

### entity-roster  <characters/, locations/, objects/>

Every entity that exists in this story. Only these ids may be used; if you need someone or something that is not here, say so rather than inventing an id.
- char-ellis-fletcher: Private detective and the story's first-person narrator. Mid-forties, methodical, wry, a former police investigator who left under a cloud.
- char-lucius-harben: The victim. A reclusive horologist and collector of rare clocks and antique weapons; lived alone with a small staff at Harben House.
- char-iris-harben: Lucius's wife. Younger than her husband, composed in public, financially and emotionally entangled in his collection and reputation.
- char-thomas-reed: Lucius's former apprentice and business partner. Expert on clocks, brusque, had recent arguments with Lucius about a disputed sale.
- char-anna-rowe: Housekeeper at Harben House. Practical, observant, the person who found the body and summoned the police.
- char-inspector-margot-lane: Local police inspector assigned to the case. Respectful of Ellis but protective of procedure; cautious about letting a private eye meddle.
- loc-harben-study: Lucius Harben's private study: a compact, well-appointed room lined with books and clocks, dominated by an ornate longcase clock and a display case of antique weapons.
- loc-harben-foyer: The small foyer outside the study; the study's only door opens into this area. The rest of Harben House is silent and oak-paneled.
- obj-longcase-clock: An ornate longcase (grandfather) clock, a prized item in Lucius's collection. It has visible hands, a striking mechanism, and an access panel in its case.
- obj-ivory-revolver: A small antique single-shot revolver from Lucius's weapon display: ivory grips, gilded barrel. At the start of the case its status (in-place/missing/found) is a question to be resolved in the investigation.
- obj-brass-key: A heavy brass key used for the study's lock. It is found in the study's lock when the room is discovered locked; custody and origin matter.
- obj-torn-note: A scrap of paper found clutched in Lucius's hand with part of a sentence visible. Its provenance and whether it is genuine or planted is in question.
- obj-black-thread: A length of thin black thread (waxed linen / monofilament) found tangled behind the clock — a small, apparently insignificant physical clue that ties into mechanical timing.
- obj-envelope: A sealed envelope found on Lucius's desk containing a terse typed threat about an upcoming sale; the handwriting on the flap is later compared to suspects.

### narrative-voice  <novel/style/voice.md>

Narration: first person, char-ellis-fletcher, past tense. This was decided for the whole book before any of it was written and does not change.
Check your own sentences against it before you stage them. Mixing a collective "we" into a third-person narration, or slipping into present tense for a scene that feels immediate, is scored as a defect and is the most common one this system has produced: seven of nine consistency errors in a measured 18,000-word manuscript were exactly this.
If you think the story genuinely needs a different voice, propose the deviation — do not simply write it.

### world-rules  <world/rules.yaml>

These govern what is TRUE. They do not say what anyone KNOWS.
A character knows a rule only where canon says so; otherwise they may be ignorant of it, wrong about it, or in the middle of working it out — and if the story is about someone discovering one of these, writing it into their thoughts early is how that story gets destroyed.

- No supernatural elements or 'impossible' physics — every action must be explainable by real mechanisms or human trickery.
- The narrator, Ellis, cannot know anything he didn't observe, be told, or reasonably infer; revelations must come by evidence or deduction shown in-scene.
- Forensic details (gunshot residue, fingerprints, time of death signs) must be internally consistent and not contradicted later.
- All significant objects, locations and characters used in scenes must be declared as entities above; later scenes may only refer to these ids.
- Locked-room constraints are physical: doors and windows can only be manipulated by plausible mechanical means or realistic sleight, and any trick must be demonstrable within the story's scenes.
- No retroactive retcons of committed facts; if a gap exists it must be acknowledged as such in the prose and can be left unresolved.

## The draft

The cab left me on a wet flagstone, the driver already counting the seconds until he could leave. Harben House sat back from the lane under a low sky; rain freckled the leaded windows and made the oak panels look younger than they were. Inspector Lane stood in the small foyer with her collar up, a constable behind her, the hall already marked off with a strip of tape that had more dignity than utility. “Don’t touch anything until forensics are here, Ellis,” she said when she saw me. Her voice was polite; her eyes were not.

Anna Rowe met me at the study door. She had been the one to find him. “I found him at his desk, Mr. Fletcher. He still had something in his hand,” she told me before she could stop herself. Her hands were steady but her knuckles were white where she gripped a shawl.

The study door was shut. A heavy brass key sat in its lock, the metal dulled by years of handling and scored along one edge. Lane pointed at it without looking: “Locked from the inside,” she said. She did not ask me whether I wanted to see; that would have been an invitation I would have taken if she had given it.

The room beyond smelled of oil and paper and a faint, sharp tang of metal. It was smaller than my head had made it; bookcases leaned in as if gossiping. The longcase clock took up the far wall, an upright thing of walnut and gilt that pulled the light toward it. Its hands were frozen at eleven seventeen; the pendulum hung motionless, a dark tongue. Whatever had stopped it had stopped it cleanly—the access panel at the rear of the case was a hair ajar, a sliver of inner brass visible where the latch sat crooked.

Opposite the clock, a glass-fronted case displayed a row of mounts on velvet. One mount was empty. A little brass label under the gap read IVORY REVOLVER in neat type; the mounting beneath it showed the ghost of a shape, the crushed velvet where the grip had rested. The case held everything else in its place, all the gilded mouths and ivory handles lined up, and then that absence like a missing tooth.

Lucius Harben sat at his desk with his shoulders folded forward as if in sleep. The back of his head caught the light; his fingers curled over a torn scrap. I stepped closer the way you do when you mean to offend nothing, and Lane let me. His chest was still. A neat, round mark on the wood, the kind a single shot makes, stained the blotter beside his hand.

In his palm was a torn note, no larger than my thumb. The fragment I could see read, simply, do not wind. I read the words twice, because a sentence like that felt like a trap or an instruction and I prefer to be polite in the face of either.

At the base of the clock, tangled in the carved scrollwork, a black thread hung, waxed and stiff. It caught my nail when I checked it; it looked absurdly ordinary to be part of anything clever, and for that reason I did not dismiss it.

The windows were latched and the glass unbroken. No sign of forced entry showed on the doorframe; the brass key remained in the lock on the study side. Anna hovered near the threshold, glancing from the body to the clock as if she were still trying to reconcile two different days. Lane watched the room the way a surgeon watches an exposed artery.

I said nothing at first. There was a set of small, precise things here: a stopped clock, a brass key in the lock, an empty space where an ivory revolver should have been, a torn note clutched in a dead man’s hand. The facts were polite and stubborn; they would have to be asked their questions in order. For now there was only the noise of the rain, the smell of oil, and the way the house seemed to be holding its breath.

## Second axis: the writing itself

The nineteen subtypes above are consistency errors, and they are one of the two numbers
this system is scored on. The other is quality, judged on rubrics that penalise things no
consistency subtype can express — and that is where our deficit actually is: measured on
the same task, our length score was the best in the field and our quality score was 0.5 to
0.8 points below the frontier on a five-point scale, where one point of quality is worth
ten points of the mean.

Two of the worst defects found by reading our finished manuscripts were invisible to a
consistency gate by construction. The story **had no ending** — the final scene was a
confrontation that named nobody and closed on "Not yet. There is enough for a warrant" —
and an unresolved ending contradicts nothing, so there was no subtype to report it as. And
the scenes **restate each other**: same content, different words, so no textual comparison
sees it, and it is not a contradiction. It is what makes a long story feel padded.

- **off_brief** (can block) — the scene does something other than what its card said it would, or drifts off what the task actually asked for — a required element of the premise handled as background, or a scene that services a thread the task never mentioned.

The cab left me on a wet flagstone, the driver already counting the seconds until he could leave. Harben House sat back from the lane under a low sky; rain freckled the leaded windows and made the oak panels look younger than they were. Inspector Lane stood in the small foyer with her collar up, a constable behind her, the hall already marked off with a strip of tape that had more dignity than utility. “Don’t touch anything until forensics are here, Ellis,” she said when she saw me. Her voice was polite; her eyes were not.

Anna Rowe met me at the study door. She had been the one to find him. “I found him at his desk, Mr. Fletcher. He still had something in his hand,” she told me before she could stop herself. Her hands were steady but her knuckles were white where she gripped a shawl.

The study door was shut. A heavy brass key sat in its lock, the metal dulled by years of handling and scored along one edge. Lane pointed at it without looking: “Locked from the inside,” she said. She did not ask me whether I wanted to see; that would have been an invitation I would have taken if she had given it.

The room beyond smelled of oil and paper and a faint, sharp tang of metal. It was smaller than my head had made it; bookcases leaned in as if gossiping. The longcase clock took up the far wall, an upright thing of walnut and gilt that pulled the light toward it. Its hands were frozen at eleven seventeen; the pendulum hung motionless, a dark tongue. Whatever had stopped it had stopped it cleanly—the access panel at the rear of the case was a hair ajar, a sliver of inner brass visible where the latch sat crooked.

Opposite the clock, a glass-fronted case displayed a row of mounts on velvet. One mount was empty. A little brass label under the gap read IVORY REVOLVER in neat type; the mounting beneath it showed the ghost of a shape, the crushed velvet where the grip had rested. The case held everything else in its place, all the gilded mouths and ivory handles lined up, and then that absence like a missing tooth.

Lucius Harben sat at his desk with his shoulders folded forward as if in sleep. The back of his head caught the light; his fingers curled over a torn scrap. I stepped closer the way you do when you mean to offend nothing, and Lane let me. His chest was still. A neat, round mark on the wood, the kind a single shot makes, stained the blotter beside his hand.

In his palm was a torn note, no larger than my thumb. The fragment I could see read, simply, do not wind. I read the words twice, because a sentence like that felt like a trap or an instruction and I prefer to be polite in the face of either.

At the base of the clock, tangled in the carved scrollwork, a black thread hung, waxed and stiff. It caught my nail when I checked it; it looked absurdly ordinary to be part of anything clever, and for that reason I did not dismiss it.

The windows were latched and the glass unbroken. No sign of forced entry showed on the doorframe; the brass key remained in the lock on the study side. Anna hovered near the threshold, glancing from the body to the clock as if she were still trying to reconcile two different days. Lane watched the room the way a surgeon watches an exposed artery.

I said nothing at first. There was a set of small, precise things here: a stopped clock, a brass key in the lock, an empty space where an ivory revolver should have been, a torn note clutched in a dead man’s hand. The facts were polite and stubborn; they would have to be asked their questions in order. For now there was only the noise of the rain, the smell of oil, and the way the house seemed to be holding its breath.

Opposite the clock the weapons case kept its quiet. One mount was empty; the brass plaque beneath read IVORY REVOLVER. The velvet where a grip had lain was pressed down, an absence that made the rest of the row look oddly whole by comparison.

On Lucius Harben’s desk a sealed envelope sat with a shallow diagonal crease across the flap. When I tilted it the typed line showed through the thin paper, blunt and plain: “DO NOT SELL THE IVORY REVOLVER. THIS IS YOUR LAST WARNING.” I did not open it; forensics would want their say.

Anna Rowe stood in the doorway, practical and steady. She told me she had seen Mr. Harben at breakfast, just after eight, that Mrs. Harben had left for town a little after nine, and that Mr. Reed had called by later and left before eleven. She reminded me she’d been the one to find him at his desk and that he’d still been holding something in his hand when she did.

She gave a neat account — she’d been in town that morning to discuss payments connected with the collection — and kept her voice level while she smoothed the edge of her hand against her wedding band. The motion was small and automatic, a private thing trying to steady public calm. She would not be drawn on the envelope; she said only that talk of sales had made her anxious for the house’s finances.

Thomas Reed was in the service room, his hands carrying the faint grains of his work. He said he’d been in the workshop across the square until just before eleven and that a neighbour could confirm it. The rear access panel was a hair ajar and the latch sat crooked where it should have been flush. At the base, tucked behind the inner brass and snagged on a small screw, a length of black thread hung, waxed and stiff. A thin line of dust lay above it; below, the wood was cleaner, as if someone had brushed the area in haste.

Opposite the clock the weapons case kept its quiet. One mount was empty; the brass plaque beneath read IVORY REVOLVER. The velvet where a grip had lain was pressed down, an absence that made the rest of the row look oddly whole by comparison.

On Lucius Harben’s desk a sealed envelope sat with a shallow diagonal crease across the flap. When I tilted it the typed line showed through the thin paper, blunt and plain: “DO NOT SELL THE IVORY REVOLVER. THIS IS YOUR LAST WARNING.” I did not open it; forensics would want their say.

Anna Rowe stood in the doorway, practical and steady. She reminded me she’d been the one to find him at his desk and that he’d still been holding something in his hand when she did.

She repeated, without irony, the warning she’d given me at the start: “Don’t touch anything until forensics are here, Ellis.” Her look after the words said I could look and ask questions, but I must not be a clumsy hand. I went back into the study with Lane's warning still in my pocket like a coin I couldn't spend. She had told me not to touch anything until forensics arrived; I kept my hands in my coat and let my eyes do the work. The longcase clock took the far wall and swallowed the light. The access panel at the back was a hair ajar; when I peered in the brass looked thumbed and raw where varnish had been rubbed away. There were fine, fresh scores around the latch—hairline marks that caught the light as if someone had used a slender tool to lever it open.

At the base the black thread hung where I'd seen it: waxed, stiff, caught on a small screw. This time I followed its line with my gaze. It wasn't a loose scrap that had wandered into the case; the thread looped and ran up toward the movement, vanishing behind the plates. If you wanted a thing to move at a chosen minute, a thread laid like that would be the sort of modest, patient device you'd use.

I didn't say any of that aloud. I turned instead to Thomas Reed when he came in from the workshop, his hands smelling faintly of oil. He had that thumb-and-forefinger rub that men in his trade do when they steady themselves. "You were in here recently?" I asked.

He met my eyes and his mouth went flat. He said, "I was in three days ago to wind it and I stripped the weight-gear to clean the pivots—it's delicate work, Ellis." The sentence landed without flourish; it was an admission and a small, professional apology all at once.

"You left the panel ajar?" I asked.

He looked past me at the frame of the clock. "No," he said. "I always close it. I wouldn't leave the case open. I closed it when I left." He rubbed his thumb harder, like a man trying to work a stubborn tooth loose. "I didn't kill him, if that's what you're getting at. I serviced it—winding, cleaning the pivots—but I was out of the shop by ten. Ask anyone." His voice tightened on the last clause.

There was a thing in the dead man's hand that didn't fit with Thomas's timeline. Lucius's fingers were curled around a torn scrap; the ragged edge lay on top of the knuckles, the torn fibres splayed against his skin rather than pressed into it. The blotter beneath showed the neat ring of a round stain, the dark halo that told you where blood had soaked through. The scrap, though, sat on that halo without a smear. If he'd clutched the paper in his last moments it would have been different—the fibres would have been pressed, ink and blood mingled into the edge. This looked staged.

"The scrap's been put there after the fact," I said, and I kept my tone light because accusation is heavy and Lane was watching. "Its fibres lie on top of his fingers. It hasn't been pressed into the skin, and there's no transfer where you'd expect it."

Thomas's cheeks hollowed. "Why would someone do that?" he asked. "To make it look—" He didn't finish.

That was when Lane walked over with the constable and a man from forensics, although they were careful and quick and didn't disturb anything more than a single gloved hand to lift a sample. The forensics man paused at the desk and tapped his latexed finger at the envelope's diagonal crease. "We lifted a partial print from the flap's crease," he told me without flourish. "Preliminary lift consistent with Iris Harben."

Iris appeared then, as if the naming had summoned her. She was composed; the movement of her hand to her wedding band was the small private motion I had seen before. When I asked her about the sale and the note she said, with a bluntness that might have been armour, "If he sells it, we have nothing left but his arrogance."

Her words settled over the room like another clock tuning itself. For a moment everything in the study felt arranged to be observed: the stopped hands at eleven-seventeen, the access panel that shouldn't have been raw with tool-marks, the thread running toward the gears, a torn note that read like stagecraft, and an envelope that now carried a print.

I kept my hands where Lane could see them and stepped to the clock's case. I did not touch the latch; forensics had the gloves and the reason. But the thing I was thinking was plain and dangerous: this wasn't just a prized object anymore. If someone's clever—or cruel—hand had used the train as a timer, the clock could be the mechanism that killed Lucius.

The nineteen subtypes above are consistency errors, and they are one of the two numbers

consistency subtype can express — and that is where our deficit actually is: measured on
the same task, our length score was the best in the field and our quality score was 0.5 to

Two of the worst defects found by reading our finished manuscripts were invisible to a
consistency gate by construction. The story **had no ending** — the final scene was a

- **off_brief** (can block) — the scene does something other than what its card said it would, or drifts off what the task actually asked for — a required element of the premise handled as background, or a scene that services a thread the task never mentioned.

Everything else is a warning — it reaches the writer and costs nothing. That asymmetry is
deliberate: a craft judgement a reader could reasonably disagree with must not be able to
hold up a scene.

And a blocking craft finding needs **checkable evidence**, in the shape the check names.

thing to do.

the manuscript, the index or the rubric. A craft note without an instruction is a complaint

first when both are present: it is counted by name and craft is not. So if you have three

I went back into the study with Lane’s caution still hanging between us. She closed the door behind her and said, in the very words she’d used when I first arrived, “Don’t touch anything until forensics are here, Ellis.” The sentence landed like a rule; her eyes supplied everything she didn’t say.

The longcase clock took the far wall and held the light. Its hands were frozen at eleven seventeen; the pendulum hung motionless. The rear access panel was a hair ajar and the latch sat crooked where it should have been flush. At the base, tucked behind the inner brass and snagged on a small screw, a length of black thread hung, waxed and stiff. A thin line of dust lay above it; below, the wood was cleaner, as if someone had brushed the area in haste.

Opposite the clock the weapons case kept its quiet. One mount was empty; the brass plaque beneath read IVORY REVOLVER. The velvet where a grip had lain was pressed down, an absence that made the rest of the row look oddly whole by comparison.

On Lucius Harben’s desk a sealed envelope sat with a shallow diagonal crease across the flap. When I tilted it the typed line showed through the thin paper, blunt and plain: “DO NOT SELL THE IVORY REVOLVER. THIS IS YOUR LAST WARNING.” I did not open it; forensics would want their say.

Anna Rowe stood in the doorway, practical and steady. She told me she had seen Mr. Harben at breakfast, just after eight, that Mrs. Harben had left for town a little after nine, and that Mr. Reed had called by later and left before eleven. She reminded me she’d been the one to find him at his desk and that he’d still been holding something in his hand when she did.

Iris Harben spoke to me in the small parlour off the foyer. She gave a neat account — she’d been in town that morning to discuss payments connected with the collection — and kept her voice level while she smoothed the edge of her hand against her wedding band. The motion was small and automatic, a private thing trying to steady public calm. She would not be drawn on the envelope; she said only that talk of sales had made her anxious for the house’s finances.

Thomas Reed was in the service room, his hands carrying the faint grains of his work. He said he’d been in the workshop across the square until just before eleven and that a neighbour could confirm it. He spoke quickly, with an impatience that shortened his answers, and kept rubbing the pad of his thumb and forefinger together in that restless way of men who handle small gears. When I asked about the disputed sale he gave a clipped account and shut the subject down.

Lane watched from the doorway as I closed matters with Thomas and then returned to the study. She repeated, without irony, the warning she’d given me at the start: “Don’t touch anything until forensics are here, Ellis.” Her look after the words said I could look and ask questions, but I must not be a clumsy hand. I told her I understood. That would have to be enough for now.

Opposite the clock, a glass-fronted case displayed a row of mounts on velvet. One mount was empty. A little brass label under the gap read IVORY REVOLVER in neat type; the mounting beneath it showed the ghost of a shape, the crushed velvet where the grip had rested. The case held everything else in its place, all the gilded mouths and ivory handles lined up, and then that absence like a missing tooth.

Lucius Harben sat at his desk with his shoulders folded forward as if in sleep. The back of his head caught the light; his fingers curled over a torn scrap. I stepped closer the way you do when you mean to offend nothing, and Lane let me. His chest was still. A neat, round mark on the wood, the kind a single shot makes, stained the blotter beside his hand.

In his palm was a torn note, no larger than my thumb. The fragment I could see read, simply, do not wind. I read the words twice, because a sentence like that felt like a trap or an instruction and I prefer to be polite in the face of either.

At the base of the clock, tangled in the carved scrollwork, a black thread hung, waxed and stiff. It caught my nail when I checked it; it looked absurdly ordinary to be part of anything clever, and for that reason I did not dismiss it.

The windows were latched and the glass unbroken. No sign of forced entry showed on the doorframe; the brass key remained in the lock on the study side. Anna hovered near the threshold, glancing from the body to the clock as if she were still trying to reconcile two different days. Lane watched the room the way a surgeon watches an exposed artery.

I said nothing at first. There was a set of small, precise things here: a stopped clock, a brass key in the lock, an empty space where an ivory revolver should have been, a torn note clutched in a dead man’s hand. The facts were polite and stubborn; they would have to be asked their questions in order. For now there was only the noise of the rain, the smell of oil, and the way the house seemed to be holding its breath.

## The draft

I went back into the study with Lane's warning folded into the hollow of a sentence I couldn't spend. She'd told me not to touch anything until forensics arrived; I left my hands in my coat and let my eyes do the work. The longcase clock took the far wall and held the light. The access panel at the back was a hair ajar; the brass inside looked thumbed, varnish rubbed away where skin or a tool had rested. Fine, fresh scores ringed the latch—hairline marks that flashed when the light caught them, as if a slender implement had been used to lever it.

At the base the black thread hung where I'd seen it: waxed, stiff, snagged on a screw. I followed its line: it looped and ran up toward the movement and vanished behind the plates. That was no stray sewing fibre; laid like that it could be a patient little mechanism, a thing that might nudge a wheel at an appointed minute.

Thomas Reed came in from the workshop, bringing the faint smell of oil with him. He had the thumb-and-forefinger rub that tells you a man is working through a thought. "You were in here recently?" I asked.

He met my gaze. "I was in three days ago to wind it and I stripped the weight-gear to clean the pivots—it's delicate work, Ellis." He paused, then added, "I was out of the shop just before eleven. Ask anyone." The admission sat in the room like a small brass cog: useful, precise, and easily checked.

"You left the panel closed?" I said.

"I always close it when I'm done," he said. He rubbed his thumb as if to work a stubborn splinter free. "I didn't kill him, if that's what you're getting at. I serviced it—winding, cleaning the pivots—but I was gone by then." His voice tightened on the last word.

Lucius's fingers curled around a torn scrap. The ragged edge lay on top of the knuckles; the torn fibres splayed against the skin rather than pressed into it. The blotter beneath showed a neat, round stain—the dark halo of a single shot. The scrap sat on that halo without a smear. If he'd clutched the paper in his last moments the fibres would have been pressed, ink and blood rubbed into the edge. This looked arranged.

"The scrap was put there after the fact," I said, careful to keep my tone even. Accusation is heavy; Lane was watching.

Thomas's face went slack. "Why would someone do that? To make it look—" He stopped.

Forensics arrived just then. They moved with the efficiency of people who practise restraint: a gloved hand to lift, a small vacuum for trace, a careful photograph. The tech at the desk tapped the envelope's diagonal crease with a latexed fingertip. "We lifted a partial print from the flap's crease," he said. "Preliminary lift consistent with Iris Harben."

Iris came in as if the name had called her. She kept her composure; the small motion of smoothing her wedding band was the private thing I'd noticed before. When I asked about the sale and the note she answered with a bluntness that might be armour. "If he sells it, we have nothing left but his arrogance."

For a moment the study felt like a display cabinet for evidence: the stopped hands at eleven-seventeen, the access panel scored with fresh marks, the black thread threading toward the gears, a torn note that read like stagecraft, and an envelope that now carried a lifted print. I kept my hands where Lane could see them and stepped to the clock's case without touching the latch. Forensics had the gloves and the reasons.

What I thought, and was careful not to say out loud, was simple and dangerous: this clock had become more than a piece on a mantel. If someone clever—or cruel—had used the train as a timer, a clock could do a very private kind of violence.

## Second axis: the writing itself

The nineteen subtypes above are consistency errors, and they are one of the two numbers
this system is scored on. The other is quality, judged on rubrics that penalise things no
consistency subtype can express — and that is where our deficit actually is: measured on
the same task, our length score was the best in the field and our quality score was 0.5 to
0.8 points below the frontier on a five-point scale, where one point of quality is worth
ten points of the mean.

Two of the worst defects found by reading our finished manuscripts were invisible to a
consistency gate by construction. The story **had no ending** — the final scene was a
confrontation that named nobody and closed on "Not yet. There is enough for a warrant" —
and an unresolved ending contradicts nothing, so there was no subtype to report it as. And
the scenes **restate each other**: same content, different words, so no textual comparison
sees it, and it is not a contradiction. It is what makes a long story feel padded.

that penalises it:

- **off_brief** (can block) — the scene does something other than what its card said it would, or drifts off what the task actually asked for — a required element of the premise handled as background, or a scene that services a thread the task never mentioned.

- **restates_prior_scene** (can block) — the scene delivers information, a realisation or a beat the reader already has. Not the same words — the same content: a suspicion re-voiced, a relationship re-explained, a clue re-found. This is what makes a long story feel padded rather than long, and verbatim overlap does not detect it.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth — "seriously lacking breadth and depth with minimal information"; LongBench-Write Reading Experience — "boring and hard to understand"
- **nothing_changes** (can block) — the situation at the end of the scene is the situation at the start. Nobody knows something new, owes something new, has lost something or has decided. Name the state at the open and the state at the close; if you cannot name a difference, that is the finding.

- **internal_incoherence** (can block) — the scene contradicts itself, with both halves inside this draft — a detail stated one way early and another way late, a character reacting to something they have not been told in this scene, a sequence that cannot have happened in the order given. This needs no index at all, which is why it is inexcusable to miss.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Accuracy — "content with numerous errors and highly misleading"; LongBench-Write Coherence
- **ending_not_delivered** (can block) — the last scene stops instead of ending. The question the premise poses is not answered on the page: who, how, and — in a mystery — how the impossibility was possible. An arrangement of clues from which a reader could deduce the answer is not the answer. Name the question the premise poses and quote where the draft answers it; if you cannot quote that, the ending is not delivered.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Accuracy and Relevance; LongStoryEval Expectation Fulfillment
- **summary_not_scene** (warning only) — events reported rather than dramatised — a paragraph that says an argument happened instead of letting it happen. Compression is legitimate and necessary; a scene whose central beat is summarised is not compressed, it is skipped.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Reading Experience; LongStoryEval Writing and Language — "the writing style's ability to engage and captivate readers"
- **thin_for_its_length** (warning only) — the scene is near its word target and carries one beat's worth of content, padded with restatement, weather, or interiority that repeats itself. The grader penalises this and the length score does not reward it.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth
- **costless_conflict** (warning only) — a conflict resolved without costing anybody anything specific. Partial and temporary resolutions are fine; free ones read as unearned.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Emotional Impact — "the story's ability to evoke strong and deep emotional impact"
- **theme_stated** (warning only) — a sentence that explains what the story means, rather than a choice that tests it. Quote the sentence — it is almost always removable without loss.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Themes — "how well the themes are explored throughout the story"
- **flat_diction** (warning only) — constructions repeating within the scene, filter verbs standing in for perception ("she felt that", "he realised that"), abstraction where a concrete detail belongs, or sentence rhythm that does not move with the tension.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Writing and Language; LongBench-Write Clarity — "confusing expression with minimal details"
- **inert_open_or_close** (warning only) — the scene opens on setting or mood rather than a situation already in motion, or closes on a mood rather than a specific next beat — an unanswered question, a door about to open. In a long story this is what decides whether the reader turns over.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Reading Experience; LongStoryEval Enjoyment and Engagement
- **genre_promise_unmet** (warning only) — the scene declines the obligation its genre carries — a horror scene with nothing at stake, a romance scene with no charge between the two people, a mystery scene that advances no inference.     penalised by: LongStoryEval Expectation Fulfillment; LongBench-Write Relevance

Two rules, both enforced by the tool rather than left to your judgement:

Only these may be **error** and therefore cost the writer a round: off_brief, restates_prior_scene, nothing_changes, internal_incoherence, ending_not_delivered.
Everything else is a warning — it reaches the writer and costs nothing. That asymmetry is
deliberate: a craft judgement a reader could reasonably disagree with must not be able to
hold up a scene.

And a blocking craft finding needs **checkable evidence**, in the shape the check names.
Either two verbatim quotes (this draft, and the earlier passage it repeats or the half of
itself it contradicts), or a named state pair — what is true when the scene opens and what
is true when it closes. `nothing_changes` is precisely the claim that you cannot name a
difference, so name both halves and let the pair be the evidence. If you cannot produce
the evidence, you have an impression: report it as a warning, which is a perfectly useful
thing to do.

`suggestion` is mandatory on every craft finding, warnings included. The writer cannot see
the manuscript, the index or the rubric. A craft note without an instruction is a complaint
it can only answer by guessing, and a guessed craft repair damages prose that was working —
which is not hypothetical: a run whose findings the writer could not act on scored 8.4
points below one with fewer, better ones.

At most two craft findings can block one round, whatever you report. Consistency comes
first when both are present: it is counted by name and craft is not. So if you have three
craft blockers, the third is a warning — pick the two that most damage the scene.

I went back into the study with Lane's warning folded into the hollow of a sentence I couldn't spend. She'd told me not to touch anything until forensics arrived; I left my hands in my coat and let my eyes do the work. The longcase clock took the far wall and held the light. The access panel at the back was a hair ajar; the brass inside looked thumbed, varnish rubbed away where skin or a tool had rested. Fine, fresh scores ringed the latch—hairline marks that flashed when the light caught them, as if a slender implement had been used to lever it.

At the base the black thread hung where I'd seen it: waxed, stiff, snagged on a screw. I followed its line: it looped and ran up toward the movement and vanished behind the plates. That was no stray sewing fibre; laid like that it could be a patient little mechanism, a thing that might nudge a wheel at an appointed minute.

Thomas Reed came in from the workshop, bringing the faint smell of oil with him. He had the thumb-and-forefinger rub that tells you a man is working through a thought. "You were in here recently?" I asked.

He met my gaze. "I was in three days ago to wind it and I stripped the weight-gear to clean the pivots—it's delicate work, Ellis." He paused, then added, "I was out of the shop just before eleven. Ask anyone." The admission sat in the room like a small brass cog: useful, precise, and easily checked.

"You left the panel closed?" I said.

"I always close it when I'm done," he said. He rubbed his thumb as if to work a stubborn splinter free. "I didn't kill him, if that's what you're getting at. I serviced it—winding, cleaning the pivots—but I was gone by then." His voice tightened on the last word.

The case held everything else in its place, all the gilded mouths and ivory handles lined up, and then that absence like a missing tooth.

I stepped closer the way you do when you mean to offend nothing, and Lane let me. His chest was still. ## The draft

I set it out on the table the way a man lays out his tools: stitch by stitch, hinge by hinge, until the thing that had looked like a miracle looked like a machine. Lane let me — or at least she let my mouth do the work while her gloves stayed where they belonged — and the room filled with the sound of explanation rather than mystery.

Start with the clock. The rear panel, the scores around the latch and the dust-line above the black thread were not theatre; they were the scaffold. Inside, behind a false rear shelf I pried free with the corner of a photograph, sat a shallow cavity the colour of old walnut. It was exactly the size a small revolver would need. "There was a false shelf inside the case, a shallow cavity exactly the dimensions the ivory's grip would have occupied," I said, and I could see the way the words landed on the faces in the room: useful and ugly.

On that shelf the revolver had not been glued or hidden like treasure; it had been bedded on a thin brass shim, trimmed to fit. The metal shaving was still there — a clean, curled sliver that matched the edge where the shim had been cut. "The ivory revolver lay on a thin brass shim inside that hollow, its gilding flecked with clock oil; a trimmed scrap of brass sat beside it," I told them. Forensics had the photographs; Lane had the look that said this was evidence and not a parable.

How it fired was the clock's dirty secret. The waxed black thread that hung at the base of the case ran up into the movement and, inside the cavity, tied to a little bent bracket that had been fastened to the gun's trigger-guard. The bracket wasn't part of the original mount; the scores around the latch and a hairline scrape where the bracket had been fixed suggested it had been added and then neatly concealed. "The thread led from the train to a tiny hook on the gun; a patient pull would have drawn the trigger," I said. Thread, hook, sear — a single patient tug at eleven-seventeen and the mechanism did the rest.

It was clever and it was ugly in equal measure. The clock would give you a moment you could trust: the strike train, wound and timed to the minute, would tug the thread. The gun, seated on the shim so its muzzle aimed at the blotter, would discharge. The pendulum's recoil and the arrangement of the shim allowed the barrel to fall back into the cavity; a catch released as the case settled, the panel closed and the latch sat crooked as if it had been turned from inside. "After the strike the gun would have been drawn back into place and the panel could be made to appear latched from within," I said. The brass key in the lock, the one Lane had pointed at the first time we'd come in, was consistent with being worked at by a loop of the same waxed thread tucked into the lock-mouth — a way to make a door look locked-from-inside without the murderer having to remain in the room.

I said these things slow because I didn't want anyone to miss them. Thomas, who had the clock in his care, put both hands in his pockets and said the thing I'd prepared for: "I didn't kill him, Ellis. I was there days ago to service the clock, but I left before eleven." It was the same humility and the same deflection he'd shown before; honest, maybe, and not what a murderer would say if he wanted to be believed.

Iris did not have the comfort of a practiced denial. I laid out the envelope — the typed threat that had been sitting on the desk — the partial lift that forensics had now confirmed, and the torn scrap from Lucius's hand that, on close inspection, had been laid on top of the knuckles after the fact. The pattern of the paper and the absence of transfer stains suggested the note had been staged. Then I said what all of it meant together: the threatened sale, the missing ivory, the envelope with her print, the cavity in the clock and the neat, surgical way the movement had been used as a timer.

Her hands smoothed at her wedding band; the small motion was the violence of habit. There was a long pause and then she said, and I could hear the smallness of it, "I couldn't let him sell it. I knew where he kept it. I did what I thought would save us." It was not a clean confession; it was a thing said to stop the explanation, not to answer it. But it was there.

Lane moved then, with that professional economy that leaves no civilities. "Mrs. Harben, you'll be formally held pending further inquiries," she said; her voice closed the distance the law needs. Thomas's mouth made the same shape of denial one more time; he met my eyes and said nothing more.

We paid off an awful kind of accounting in that study: the revolver was found and photographed in the clock's cavity; the thread, the shim scrap, the bracket and the lock loop all suggested a single plan. One piece was still missing — a small cameo watch from Mrs. Harben's mother's display, the sort of thing a family keeps for reasons that have nothing to do with money and everything to do with memory. It was not where she'd said it would be.

I folded the cameo into a pocket like a question I was not ready to answer. "I'll find it," I told the room, and Lane's look said she neither approved nor objected. Some things the law takes; some things it leaves you to find.

The nineteen subtypes above are consistency errors, and they are one of the two numbers

consistency subtype can express — and that is where our deficit actually is: measured on
the same task, our length score was the best in the field and our quality score was 0.5 to

Two of the worst defects found by reading our finished manuscripts were invisible to a
consistency gate by construction. The story **had no ending** — the final scene was a
confrontation that named nobody and closed on "Not yet. There is enough for a warrant" —
and an unresolved ending contradicts nothing, so there was no subtype to report it as. And

sees it, and it is not a contradiction. It is what makes a long story feel padded.

- **off_brief** (can block) — the scene does something other than what its card said it would, or drifts off what the task actually asked for — a required element of the premise handled as background, or a scene that services a thread the task never mentioned.

- **restates_prior_scene** (can block) — the scene delivers information, a realisation or a beat the reader already has. Not the same words — the same content: a suspicion re-voiced, a relationship re-explained, a clue re-found. This is what makes a long story feel padded rather than long, and verbatim overlap does not detect it.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth — "seriously lacking breadth and depth with minimal information"; LongBench-Write Reading Experience — "boring and hard to understand"

Only these may be **error** and therefore cost the writer a round: off_brief, restates_prior_scene, nothing_changes, internal_incoherence, ending_not_delivered.
Everything else is a warning — it reaches the writer and costs nothing. That asymmetry is
deliberate: a craft judgement a reader could reasonably disagree with must not be able to
hold up a scene.

At most two craft findings can block one round, whatever you report. Consistency comes
first when both are present: it is counted by name and craft is not. So if you have three
craft blockers, the third is a warning — pick the two that most damage the scene.

I went back into the study with Lane's warning folded into the hollow of a sentence I couldn't spend. She'd told me not to touch anything until forensics arrived; I left my hands in my coat and let my eyes do the work. The longcase clock took the far wall and held the light. The access panel at the back was a hair ajar; the brass inside looked thumbed, varnish rubbed away where skin or a tool had rested. Fine, fresh scores ringed the latch—hairline marks that flashed when the light caught them, as if a slender implement had been used to lever it.

At the base the black thread hung where I'd seen it: waxed, stiff, snagged on a screw. I followed its line: it looped and ran up toward the movement and vanished behind the plates. That was no stray sewing fibre; laid like that it could be a patient little mechanism, a thing that might nudge a wheel at an appointed minute.

Thomas Reed came in from the workshop, bringing the faint smell of oil with him. He had the thumb-and-forefinger rub that tells you a man is working through a thought. "You were in here recently?" I asked.

He met my gaze. "I was in three days ago to wind it and I stripped the weight-gear to clean the pivots—it's delicate work, Ellis." He paused, then added, "I was out of the shop just before eleven. Ask anyone." The admission sat in the room like a small brass cog: useful, precise, and easily checked.

"You left the panel closed?" I said.

"I always close it when I'm done," he said. He rubbed his thumb as if to work a stubborn splinter free. "I didn't kill him, if that's what you're getting at. I serviced it—winding, cleaning the pivots—but I was gone by then." His voice tightened on the last word.

Lucius's fingers curled around a torn scrap. The ragged edge lay on top of the knuckles; the torn fibres splayed against the skin rather than pressed into it. The blotter beneath showed a neat, round stain—the dark halo of a single shot. The scrap sat on that halo without a smear. If he'd clutched the paper in his last moments the fibres would have been pressed, ink and blood rubbed into the edge. This looked arranged.

"The scrap was put there after the fact," I said, careful to keep my tone even. Accusation is heavy; Lane was watching.

Thomas's face went slack. "Why would someone do that? To make it look—" He stopped.

Forensics arrived just then. They moved with the efficiency of people who practise restraint: a gloved hand to lift, a small vacuum for trace, a careful photograph. The tech at the desk tapped the envelope's diagonal crease with a latexed fingertip. "We lifted a partial print from the flap's crease," he said. "Preliminary lift consistent with Iris Harben."

Iris came in as if the name had called her. She kept her composure; the small motion of smoothing her wedding band was the private thing I'd noticed before. When I asked about the sale and the note she answered with a bluntness that might be armour. "If he sells it, we have nothing left but his arrogance."

For a moment the study felt like a display cabinet for evidence: the stopped hands at eleven-seventeen, the access panel scored with fresh marks, the black thread threading toward the gears, a torn note that read like stagecraft, and an envelope that now carried a lifted print. I kept my hands where Lane could see them and stepped to the clock's case without touching the latch. Forensics had the gloves and the reasons.

What I thought, and was careful not to say out loud, was simple and dangerous: this clock had become more than a piece on a mantel. If someone clever—or cruel—had used the train as a timer, a clock could do a very private kind of violence.

The study door was shut. A heavy brass key sat in its lock, the metal dulled by years of handling and scored along one edge. Lane pointed at it without looking: “Locked from the inside,” she said. She did not ask me whether I wanted to see; that would have been an invitation I would have taken if she had given it.

The room beyond smelled of oil and paper and a faint, sharp tang of metal. It was smaller than my head had made it; bookcases leaned in as if gossiping. The longcase clock took up the far wall, an upright thing of walnut and gilt that pulled the light toward it. Its hands were frozen at eleven seventeen; the pendulum hung motionless, a dark tongue. Whatever had stopped it had stopped it cleanly—the access panel at the rear of the case was a hair ajar, a sliver of inner brass visible where the latch sat crooked.

Opposite the clock, a glass-fronted case displayed a row of mounts on velvet. One mount was empty. A little brass label under the gap read IVORY REVOLVER in neat type; the mounting beneath it showed the ghost of a shape, the crushed velvet where the grip had rested. The case held everything else in its place, all the gilded mouths and ivory handles lined up, and then that absence like a missing tooth.

Lucius Harben sat at his desk with his shoulders folded forward as if in sleep. The back of his head caught the light; his fingers curled over a torn scrap. I stepped closer the way you do when you mean to offend nothing, and Lane let me. His chest was still. A neat, round mark on the wood, the kind a single shot makes, stained the blotter beside his hand.

In his palm was a torn note, no larger than my thumb. The fragment I could see read, simply, do not wind. I read the words twice, because a sentence like that felt like a trap or an instruction and I prefer to be polite in the face of either.

At the base of the clock, tangled in the carved scrollwork, a black thread hung, waxed and stiff. It caught my nail when I checked it; it looked absurdly ordinary to be part of anything clever, and for that reason I did not dismiss it.

The windows were latched and the glass unbroken. No sign of forced entry showed on the doorframe; the brass key remained in the lock on the study side. Anna hovered near the threshold, glancing from the body to the clock as if she were still trying to reconcile two different days. Lane watched the room the way a surgeon watches an exposed artery.

I said nothing at first. There was a set of small, precise things here: a stopped clock, a brass key in the lock, an empty space where an ivory revolver should have been, a torn note clutched in a dead man’s hand. The facts were polite and stubborn; they would have to be asked their questions in order. For now there was only the noise of the rain, the smell of oil, and the way the house seemed to be holding its breath.

I said it out slow, because the room needed slow sentences. Lane let my voice do the work while the techs kept their gloves on and their gloved hands where they belonged.

Forensics pried free a false rear shelf and photographed it; a technician eased a gloved finger into the gap and, after a careful shot, showed me the pictures. The images, and what the tech described, made the rest plain: a shallow cavity sat behind the shelf, the exact dimensions a small revolver's grip would have occupied. "There was a false shelf inside the case, a shallow cavity exactly the size the ivory's grip would have filled," I said, because saying it made it a thing we could look at instead of a story I was telling myself.

Photographs showed the revolver seated on a thin brass shim, its gilding marked with clock oil, a neat curled shaving of brass beside it where the shim had been trimmed. The waxed black thread that had been threaded into the movement ran into that cavity and was fastened to a small bent bracket on the gun's trigger-guard. The scores and hairline scrapes around the access panel suggested the bracket had been fitted and the work concealed.

Putting those pieces together suggested the mechanism. The clock's strike train would deliver a reliable tug at a set minute; the thread, fixed to the bracket, would pull the trigger. The revolver, bedded on the trimmed shim, could discharge toward the blotter. The shim's trimmed edge and the cavity's profile, as seen in the photographs, were consistent with a rebound that allowed the barrel to slip partly back into the hollow; a small notch or catch beneath the barrel could then take a rim as the case settled, leaving the access panel to sit crooked as if latched from inside. Those were not miracles — the photographs and the bracket's thread attachment suggested a plain, mechanical series of events.

I kept to the evidence because Lane's warning was still a thing I'd agreed to: don't touch until forensics. I did not touch. I described what their hands had revealed.

Thomas, who'd serviced the clock, rubbed his thumb and forefinger the way he always did and said the thing I'd already been given to expect: "I didn't kill him, Ellis. I was there days ago to service the clock, but I left before eleven." His admission of recent access was a cog in the machine of motive and opportunity, but his words were the same ones he'd given me before.

I set out the paper trail. The typed envelope on the desk bore the blunt warning about the ivory; forensics had lifted a partial print from the flap's diagonal crease that they described as consistent with Iris Harben. The torn scrap in Lucius's hand, on inspection, had the look of being placed afterward — fibres lying on top of the knuckles, no transfer staining. The pattern of those facts together suggested staging: a threat that tied to a sale, a missing ivory, a note put in place to mislead.

Iris's hand found her wedding band as if by habit. There was no theatrical refusal in her face; there was the small, unbearable plainness of someone calculating loss and risk. I said, without flourish, what the collection and the clock and the threat all meant together.

She answered in a voice that did not bother to be theatrical: "I couldn't let him sell it. I knew where he kept it. I did what I thought would save us." It wasn't the clean, legal confession a court prefers; it was a thing said to stop me explaining.
